extraction.name: MMMU
extraction.description: A massive multi-discipline multimodal benchmark of 11.5K college-level questions from exams, quizzes, and textbooks across six disciplines, designed to evaluate expert-level multimodal understanding and reasoning.
extraction.creator: Xiang Yue, Yuansheng Ni, Kai Zhang, Tianyu Zheng, Ruoqi Liu, Ge Zhang, Samuel Stevens, Dongfu Jiang, Weiming Ren, Yuxuan Sun, Cong Wei, Botao Yu, Ruibin Yuan, Renliang Sun, Ming Yin, Boyuan Zheng, Zhenzhu Yang, Yibo Liu, Wenhao Huang, Huan Sun, Yu Su, Wenhu Chen
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The benchmark was curated in three stages: selecting subjects based on common use of visual inputs, recruiting over 50 university students to collect multimodal questions from textbooks and online resources and create new questions when necessary, and applying multi-stage quality control including deduplication, format/typo checking, and difficulty filtering.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: College exams, quizzes, textbooks, online sources, and lecture materials.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Potential duplicates were identified using lexical overlap and source URL similarity, then reviewed and removed; problems were standardized for format and typos; authors assigned difficulty levels and excluded about 10% of very easy problems.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Data cleaning included duplicate detection and removal, standardized format and typo correction, and filtering out very easy questions that did not meet benchmark design criteria.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Over 50 university students specializing in the selected majors collected multimodal questions from textbooks and online resources and created new questions when necessary. Annotators were instructed to follow copyright and license regulations and to avoid questions with immediately available answers to reduce contamination.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Authors reviewed suspected duplicates, checked formatting and typos, categorized problems into four difficulty levels, and later analyzed 150 randomly sampled GPT-4V error instances by expert annotators to identify root causes.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 50 university students specializing in the selected majors; 90 college senior students were also involved as human experts for evaluation, with 3 student experts per subject.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: A version change log exists in the supplementary material, and the leaderboard is live-updating.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark is intended to help monitor progress toward Expert AGI, which the paper links to risks of job displacement and economic disruption, and the authors believe it can stimulate development of next-generation multimodal foundation models.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The manual curation process may carry biases.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The benchmark may carry manual curation biases, focuses only on college-level subjects, and is not sufficient by itself to test Expert AGI because there is no direct mapping to the 90th percentile of skilled adults and college exams are not the only relevant tasks.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking and evaluating multimodal models on zero-shot and few-shot multimodal understanding and reasoning; includes development, validation, and test splits, with the validation set useful for hyperparameter selection.

name.evidence: We introduce MMMU : a new benchmark designed to evaluate multimodal models on massive multi-discipline tasks demanding college-level subject knowledge and deliberate reasoning.

description.evidence: MMMU includes 11.5K meticulously collected multimodal questions from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks, covering six core disciplines: Art & Design, Business, Science, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: Data Collection. Our benchmark collection takes three stages. Firstly, we go through the common university majors to decide what subjects should be included in our benchmark... In the second stage, we recruit over 50 university students, including co-authors, specializing in these majors as annotators to assist in question collection. They collect multimodal questions from major textbooks and online resources, creating new questions based on their expertise where necessary... Data Quality Control. To further control the quality of our data, we perform two steps of data cleaning... In the third and final stage, the authors categorize the problems into four difficulty levels: very easy, easy, medium, and hard. Approximately 10% of the problems, classified as very easy and not aligning with our design criteria due to their simplistic nature, are excluded from the benchmark.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: The questions in our benchmark were manually collected by a team of 50 college students (including coauthors) from various disciplines and subjects, drawing from online sources, textbooks, and lecture materials.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: MMMU includes 11.5K meticulously collected multimodal questions from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks... The questions in our benchmark were manually collected by a team of 50 college students (including coauthors) from various disciplines and subjects, drawing from online sources, textbooks, and lecture materials.

rai:dataManipulationProtocol.evidence: In the first stage, lexical overlap and source URL similarity are employed to identify potential duplicate problems. These suspected duplicates were then reviewed by the authors to identify and eliminate any duplications. The second stage involves distributing the problems among different co-authors for format and typo checking... In the third and final stage, the authors categorize the problems into four difficulty levels: very easy, easy, medium, and hard. Approximately 10% of the problems, classified as very easy and not aligning with our design criteria due to their simplistic nature, are excluded from the benchmark.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: To further control the quality of our data, we perform two steps of data cleaning... This step requires authors to ensure adherence to a standardized format, undertaking necessary corrections where deviations are found... Approximately 10% of the problems, classified as very easy and not aligning with our design criteria due to their simplistic nature, are excluded from the benchmark.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: In the second stage, we recruit over 50 university students, including co-authors, specializing in these majors as annotators to assist in question collection. They collect multimodal questions from major textbooks and online resources, creating new questions based on their expertise where necessary. The annotators are instructed to adhere to copyright and license regulations, avoiding data from sites prohibiting copy and redistribution. Given the arising data contamination concems of foundation models, the annotators are advised to select questions without immediately available answers, such as those with answers in separate documents or at the end of textbooks.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: These suspected duplicates were then reviewed by the authors to identify and eliminate any duplications... In the third and final stage, the authors categorize the problems into four difficulty levels: very easy, easy, medium, and hard... We meticulously examine 150 randomly sampled error instances from GPT-4V’s predictions. These instances are analyzed by expert annotators who identify the root causes of mispredictions based on their knowledge and the golden explanations if available.

rai:annotatorDemographics.evidence: we recruit over 50 university students, including co-authors, specializing in these majors as annotators to assist in question collection... Human Experts. We involve 90 college senior students, selected to represent a wide range of experts in the corresponding 30 subjects (3 student experts per subject).

rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan.evidence: J. Version Change Log 119... The live-updating leaderboard is available at: https://mmmu-benchmark.github.io/#leaderboard

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: AI system that reaches “at least 90th percentile of skilled adults” in a broad range of tasks, thus starting to achieve “the substitution threshold for machine intelligence in lieu of human labor” for many industries, leading to significant risks of job displacement and economic disruption. Therefore, it is of both intellectual and societal importance to closely monitor the progress towards Expert AGI... We believe MMMU will stimulate the community to build next-generation multimodal foundation models towards expert artificial general intelligence.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: MMMU, like any benchmark, has limitations despite its comprehensive nature. The manual curation process may carry biases

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: We shall caution that MMMU is not a sufficient test for Expert AGI, as per the definition [57], because there lacks a direct mapping between performance on MMMU and “90th percentile of skilled adults,” nor are college exams the only tasks an AGI shall tackle... MMMU, like any benchmark, has limitations despite its comprehensive nature. The manual curation process may carry biases, and the focus on college-level subjects might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI [57].

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: We introduce MMMU : a new benchmark designed to evaluate multimodal models on massive multi-discipline tasks demanding college-level subject knowledge and deliberate reasoning... MMMU , constituting 11.5K questions, is divided into a few-shot development set, a validation set, and a test set. The few-shot development set includes 5 questions per subject, and the validation set, useful for hyperparameter selection, contains approximately 900 questions, while the test set comprises 10.5K questions... Our evaluation is conducted under a zero-shot setting
